speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Hon. members have, of course, expressed the desire to take a moment to pay tribute to the late Real Caouette and it is certainly appropriate that that be done forthwith. Perhaps I can then attempt to exercise some discretion in safeguarding the ordinary routine proceedings after such tributes have been paid.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House is mourning one of its most remarkable and most respected members, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). The news of his death has, I am sure, spread general consternation among us.
The name of Real Caouette will always be associated with the Social Credit Party of Canada which he inspired and led until failing health forced him to resign his post, barely a few months ago. We knew he was seriously ill, but because we remembered his astonishing energy, because we had grown used to his extraordinary vitality, we hardly believed his absence was final.
Mr. Speaker, the House will no longer have the pleasure or the benefit of the so colourful, so stirring, and at times so disarming interventions of Real Caouette. But under the sprightliness, the wit, the jest of his repartees, and throughout full-bodied and lusty speech, he remained imperturbably serious. It was the seriousness of his political convictions, that of the commitment he had made, once and for all, towards the people in the days when, without resources other than heroic energy and contagious enthusiasm, he was building a party that would play a considerable role on the federal political scene.
The representative value of his opinions can hardly be doubted: a whole sector of the working classes saw themselves in him as in a mirror at once faithful, ardent, and generator of hope and enthusiasm.

Thus, Mr. Speaker, the late member for Temiscamingue linked himself very closely to the people he strived so hard to serve, according to his interpretation of their aspirations. Thus was he deeply and solidly rooted in his province. Real Caouette's attachment for his region and for Quebec was embedded in the broader context of our country as a whole. Everywhere in Canada, which he dreamed of as a bilingual country, he had friends and was cordially received. Despite his
unswerving personal orthodoxy, he was open-minded. He was very much alive to every dimension of Canada, including of course the political dimensions of parliamentarianism and federalism. I wish here to pay a warm tribute to an authentic Canadian, Real Caouette.

Mr. Speaker, I invite hon. members to join me in extending the sincere condolences of the House to Mr. Caouette's family.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to join in and associate myself and my party with the tribute just offered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). [Translation]
The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) passed away after a long illness. To us his departure means the loss of a colleague and a friend, and to Canada as a whole the loss of a great political leader. Driven by dynamism, the hon. member for Temiscamingue had been able to renew the vitality of his party. He always worked to strengthen Canadian unity.

I think that one of the qualities of Real Caouette which was most evident to those of us who were privileged to know and to work with him was his remarkable ability to recognize and respond to the needs and hopes of Canadians who perhaps had some sense of feeling, at least, outside the systems and institutions of the government of Canada. He brought that firm commitment to their interests and their hopes into this Chamber, served it in the best traditions of parliamentary democracy, and established a standard of responsiveness to the people he served that is a model to all of us.
[DOT] (DIO)

In my own name and on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to extend our most sincere condolences to his family and his relatives.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party I should like to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in paying tribute to the memory of Real Caouette, and in extending our deepest sympathy to the members of his party and, particularly, to his family.
Like my friend, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), I remember when Real Caouette first came into this House following a byelection in 1946 and took

December 17, 1976
The Late Real Caouette
his place in the back rows of the Social Credit Party. At that time his message was a rather strong one. We wondered about it in this House, and we wondered if even the Social Credit Party of that day could take it, but history has proven that not only could his party take that message, but that he had what it took to become the leader of that movement. I know from personal conversation with him that, although his parliamentary career is best known for the years since 1962, he was always very happy about the three years he was here back in the 1940's because they enabled him to know what this place was all about.
As others have said, we are aware of his deep commitment to the social, economic and, particularly, monetary views he held. We know of his effort to speak for the underprivileged and the little people of this country in all parts of Canada, and we remember that with deep appreciation. We are also conscious of the fact that in more recent years he became an outspoken advocate of one Canada and of federalism. In particular, we appreciate the leadership he gave in his own province of Quebec. He will, indeed, be missed and we are pleased to join with others in paying our tribute to him today. We think of him also, at least those of us who are in this House, as a very warmhearted personal friend. Indeed, we shall miss him.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I wish to extend our most sincere condolences to the Caouette family.

Mr. Speaker, because the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) is on tour and was unable to come to the House this morning, he has asked me to act on his behalf to pay tribute to the man who was our leader for a very long time and to tell all my colleagues of the House how touched he was to receive the messages of all his colleagues who were able to reach him by phone or otherwise.
First, I would like to thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, after learning about the death of Mr. Caouette last evening, asked for the proceedings of the House to be adjourned at eight o'clock as a sign of mourning. He should be thanked for this action, and I do so on behalf of my party and the Caouette family.
Mr. Speaker, what has just been said by the right hon. Prime Minister and the spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party about Mr. Caouette has profoundly touched me. These words were obviously spoken sincerely. Of course, throughout his political life, Mr. Caouette always fought for an ideal. He wanted to bring about changes in Canadian society by proposing economic and monetary formulas in which he truly believed. I was associated with Mr. Caouette for many years. We knew each other since 1941, when he and I took part together in activities to promote Social Credit and convince the greatest possible number of people throughout Canada, to explain this transformation and propose it to Parliament.

It is rather rare that a political party is able to achieve its objectives under the same leader, but we must recognize that Mr. Caouette never gave up. The last time I visited him in hospital, he gave me this message as I left him: Continue to work in the same direction and for the same ideal. He also said: The Social Credit Party of Canada is not Real Caouette, it is a doctrine, it is a political philosophy. Continue to be faithful to this philosophy and to defend it as best you can. Of course, Mr. Caouette certainly did not please everyone. Like all politicians, he fought some rather hard battles. He had a colourful way of speaking and was outspoken, as the right hon. Prime Minister said a while ago. Mr. Caouette spoke his mind simply and frankly, and said the same things all over the country. This is why, today, people recognize that Mr. Caouette, by his activities and his thoughts, was a great Canadian, a man who worked with all his heart for Canadian unity.
Is it with a lot of emotion that I speak from the very same place as Mr. Caouette did when he spoke for the last time in the House last July when he took part in a very important debate. Once again, he had put his finger on what Canadians expect from Parliament, and we could say that he knew that it was his last speech in the House of Commons, because his message showed the experience of a man who had a very great vision of what our country must be.
Mr. Speaker, First of all I want to thank you for your kindness towards our leader and his family and I also want to thank the government and all my colleagues in the House for the tribute they paid to this great Canadian figure.
In conclusion, I should like to extend our heartfelt sympathy to Mrs. Caouette and to her children, and also to Mr. Caouette's brothers and sisters with whom I have close ties, and I know to what extent this family was united. I do hope that Mr. Caouette's example will be followed because he always endeavoured to defend the rights of the family and those of low income people. We were convinced of his vocation because he was himself convinced of what he said and he took the means to reach his objective. The thing we will recall about his life is that he was a hard worker, a man who understood that work is a tool to be used to fulfill one's objectives. He gave us this example, and I am convinced that my colleagues will join me in saying and repeating to all the people we shall meet: follow the example of Real Caouette by working and courageously defending your positions and your ideas, and you cannot go wrong.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. Before pursuing the business of the House, I should like to extend my personal sympathy to Mr. Caouette's family, even if in such circumstances it is always difficult to add to what has already been said by the leaders of the parties in the House.

Like many others, I am able to recall a personal relationship with this great Canadian beginning with my first days in the House and on through various responsibilities to the day when
December 17, 1976

I was elected to this position. In any exchanges, even in his formal remarks which were most kind, the attitude always adopted and expressed by this great veteran of the House of Commons was that, since he and I were northerners, we had to work together. That was a great compliment to me from a man who had been here for so many years and had such a brilliant career when I was a new member of the House. No matter how sparkling or spectacular his career became, he always identified himself with all members of the House regardless of their rank, which speaks of his brilliance and of his kindness at the same time.
I think, when paying tribute to a man of this sort, that there are occasions when nice things are said about someone only after he has passed away, but in this case it should be remembered that all during his career and during his lifetime, regardless of disagreements on theories and political philosophies which he espoused so dearly and kept so close to his heart, there was never a time when anyone had anything unkind to say about him. Not only for his oratory and spectacular political career, but for the kind of gentleman he always was, he will be sorely missed.
Hear, hear!

BASIS ON WHICH SWINE INFLUENZA VACCINATION PROGRAM SUSPENDED-CANADIAN INVESTIGATION OF EFFECTS OF VACCINATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the fact that he has made an announcement outside the House that the swine 'flu vaccination program is temporarily suspended, I wonder whether he would care to inform the House what scientific evidence he had to back up his decision to take that action.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: BASIS ON WHICH SWINE INFLUENZA VACCINATION PROGRAM SUSPENDED-CANADIAN INVESTIGATION OF EFFECTS OF VACCINATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the action we have taken in Canada results from the decision in the United States which was based on concern about complications resulting from their vaccination program. In Canada there has been no reported case of neurological complication arising out of the Canadian vaccination program. However, we consulted with all the members of the National Advisory Committee on Immunizing Agents who could be reached and with Dr. Rhodes, who may be termed the dean emeritus of public health in Canada, and received their unanimous recommendation for the following proposal, that is, to proceed with vaccination only of people over 65 and of those with chronic diseases only for the time being and to suspend vaccination of other citizens until we get further information and reports from the analysis made in the United States.

subtopic: BASIS ON WHICH SWINE INFLUENZA VACCINATION PROGRAM SUSPENDED-CANADIAN INVESTIGATION OF EFFECTS OF VACCINATION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister tell the House what measures he intends to take to clarify the question of whether there is any danger of Guillain-Barre syndrome being contracted by Canadians who underwent the vaccination against swine flu? In other words, do we have an epidemiological team of some kind investigating this or are we simply waiting for the results of the United States study?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: BASIS ON WHICH SWINE INFLUENZA VACCINATION PROGRAM SUSPENDED-CANADIAN INVESTIGATION OF EFFECTS OF VACCINATION
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. Right after launching the vaccination program, we asked all the provinces to establish a detailed examination and reporting system concerning any complications which might result from the vaccination. I must say that up to now, we did not receive any report in Canada concerning the disease called Guillain-Barre syndrome. This is the present situation. I repeat that a monitoring system has been established since the beginning of the vaccination program and so far no case of this syndrome has been reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):

subtopic: INCIDENCE OF GUILLAIN-BARRE SYNDROME AMONGST VACCINATED POPULATION OF UNITED STATES
speechtext: According to the information I got, 51 cases of the Guillain-Barre syndrome were reported as of yesterday among the 40 million persons vaccinated up to now. REASON FOR CONTINUED USE OF BIVALENT INFLUENZA VACCINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of the alleged possible dangers inherent in this monovalent swine flu vaccine, why does the department continue to condone the inconsistency of allowing the use of the bivalent vaccine? Is the reason in part that the government failed to make provision for production of the monovalent type?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REASON FOR CONTINUED USE OF BIVALENT INFLUENZA VACCINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, once again I must remind the hon. member that the Canadian vaccine supply is not the same as in United States. Our vaccine was not produced in the U.S.A. Secondly, no case of Guillain-Barre syndrome has been reported in Canada. Moreover, the Victoria flu has already appeared in North America this season and, as the hon. member knows, last spring over 3,000 Canadian citizens died from this type of flu within six weeks. Experts therefore concluded that the death hazard was much higher with the Victoria flu than with the possible effect of Guillain-Barre syndrome complications.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASE IN INTERNATIONAL PRICE OF OIL-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO COUNTERACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Finance? It concerns the announcement of a majority of the OPEC countries to the effect that they intend to raise the price of oil by 10 per cent in the early part of next year and another 5 per cent later in the year. In view of the fact that a 10 per cent increase in the price of petroleum in this country would cost consumers an additional $700 million per year, and in view of the fact that the minister is reported as saying that "this is an increase we can manage; that the Canadian economy can handle it and that for us it is not a life or death situation", may I ask him what steps the government proposes to take to meet this situation which could have a depressing effect on the economy and result in a further slowdown in any economic recovery?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASE IN INTERNATIONAL PRICE OF OIL-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO COUNTERACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just point out to the hon. gentleman that the passage he quoted was in a passage which referred to the impact on the non-oil-producing, less-developing countries about whom I said this was literally a matter of life and death and this was the reason for opposing the increase. I would remind him that the OPEC oil increase of itself will not have an impact upon petroleum users in Canada in the near future. The price within Canada is set in accordance with the Petroleum Administration Act. The additional costs of oil being delivered principally to the eastern Canadian market, while they will increase for the refineries, will be cushioned by the subvention the government pays in order to keep down the Canadian price. I should note at the same time that by the agreement established earlier this year there will be an oil price increase in Canada as of January 1, but it will not be caused by OPEC action.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT PUBLIC BE ASSURED INDEXED PENSION PLAN NOT BURDEN ON TAXPAYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to give the hon. member and the House the assurance that it is our determined intention to examine this plan. When we complete the final review of it, we will make sure that there is no taxpayer subsidy to cover excessive payroll costs of the pension plan. I would refer the hon. member to the document I tabled in the House, I believe on October 18, the "Basic Facts about Pensions in the Public Service of Canada", which indicated that if the long-term relationship between wages, interest and inflation is maintained, payroll costs through to the year 2025 would in fact be similar to what they have been in the last several years.
I want to assure the House that those payroll costs, projected and experienced in this plan, very favourably compare with those of pension plans in the private sector; nevertheless we are reviewing the situation thoroughly. In the course of that review I am very interested in getting an independent actuarial analysis of the plan to test, check and confirm the assumptions and calculations that went into the document which has been circulated.

The House resumed, from Wesdnesday, December 15, consideration in committee of Bill C-22, to amend the statute law relating to income tax-Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale)-Mr. Laniel in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the House rose on Wednesday, December 15, clause 1 of the bill was under consideration.
On clause 1.

Mr. Chairman, I want to reinforce very briefly the point that was made by the hon. member for Red Deer on Wednesday. I draw particular attention to a problem that affects many members in the federal House and provincial legislatures where there are changes in what is the equivalent to retirement savings plans. Some are also registered pension plans. The same principle applies. It applies particularly to the registered retirement savings plan. Under the legislation which affects the pension plans, they are changed from time to time; they are upgraded. It is a requirement that full participation shall bring in a considerable amount of arrears. We saw this with the increase in the level from $2,500 to $3,500. There was the current instalment plus the allocated portion of arrears up to $2,500 or, at present $3,500. There was some ambivalence in the tax department with regard to that. It resulted in some hardships. I know I was caught in it. One year we were allowed an excess. As I pointed out, it was a requirement of law to make this payment and we were paying toward arrears. The following year the then minister of national revenue denied the claim and taxed on the excess over $2,500, now over $3,500. Not only that, he had the gall to reassess for one year with interest and penalties. Although the information was volunteered, and the tax authorities re-examined their previous decision, I can say that I know it also happened to some of my colleagues. This happens across the country.
If there is an overpayment, it is a requirement of the plan, by law, that the excess shall be subject to tax. When either the
December 17, 1976

registered retirement savings plan or the pension plan comes into play, that same money is again taxed. It is taxed twice. I agree that it is a matter of policy that contributions to pension plans shall be limited. However, a person who has a higher income may certainly have earned it and earned it very well, just as capably as the man who only has a $10,000 salary. Just because he has a salary of $75,000 and works twice as hard, he is penalized.
Half as hard.

In many cases he works twice or three times as hard, but suffers the penalty, for being industrious. There is this limit for both the retirement pension plan and the registered retirement savings plan. There should be a change in order to avoid this anomaly of double-taxation. I admit there is a provision where there is fluctuating income and that any excess in one year can be carried forward to fill the void of some deficiencies in the limit in subsequent years. However, that never happens under the plans about which I am speaking. I would like to hear from the minister the justification for the double-taxation on these excess contributions which, incidentally, are made under law and are not a matter of individual choice.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member knows, the law provides for a certain maximum on contributions to a program. Where an individual's program is enriched, either voluntarily or involuntarily, it is suggested he be allowed to claim the additional payment against his income in the year of paying back for previous years. That, in effect, would allow him to have a greater tax exemption than would have been possible in those past years. In other words, by paying up for years past he would be able to get a better tax break than if he had been paying on the higher level all the way through. In that sense it would be inequitable to other taxpayers. It is inherent in a certain amount being deductible from tax income for this purpose.

Mr. Chairman, when we were interrupted in our discussion on clause 1 by three knocks on the door on Wednesday afternoon, I believe I was discussing this matter and putting a particular question to the Minister of Finance. The discussion on clause 1 of this bill, which has to do with RRSPs, has not only ranged all over the lot but has gone from one extreme to the other. There are those who seem to think that RRSPs are the answer to inadequate retirement income and that the conditions pertaining to them should be improved. There are others who think that RRSPs are mainly a bonanza to those in the upper income brackets and hardly worth all the time we are giving them.
The minister, in response to some of the questions that have been put to him, has referred to an over-all study of pensions being made by a special committee on which, I believe, three departments are represented, the Department of Finance, the Department of National Health and Welfare, and the Trea-
Income Tax
sury Board. It is good to know that such an over-all study is being made, but there is a point I should like to make as I put my question, namely, that there is a particular view about pensions which I think should now be considered very seriously. It is a point of view which says that RRSPs are not the answer to the problem and that certain other things are not the answer either. That point of view is that when retired persons receive pensions, they are not really living on their savings- they are not living on food, clothing, shelter and other services which they have saved. They are living by consuming things that are currently produced.
In other words, pensions, in the final analysis, are paid, at the time they are paid, out of the wealth that is produced at that time. This being the case, I should like to make the point that more consideration should be given to pay-as-you-go pension plans and that consideration be given to doing away with pension funds or so-called pension accounts.
I said the other day that I would call the hon. member for Eglinton as a witness-he was in the House at the time-and I said that because back in the days when he was minister of finance and I was making this point he expressed agreement with me that funds are somewhat of a delusion, or at least a fiction, and I think I am fair to him when I say that.
Let me cite the government's experience. When we first adopted old age security which became effective in 1952, since it was a new, grand scheme, so much better than the old age pensions which we had had for many years before that, it was established on the basis of a fund, and we carried on that fund for a number of years. We had special taxes, the revenues from which went into that fund. In the meantime, having raised those taxes by several percentage points, after a while we did away with those special taxes but provided for a transfer from general tax revenue to the old age security fund. But later we did away with that arrangement altogether. We now admit that the money that is paid to senior citizens as old age security is strictly on a pay as you go basis; it is money or wealth that is created today paid to people who are now retired. I suggest that it is the best and most logical form of pension payments.
You get the other extreme by looking at the government operation in plans such as the public service superannuation plan or the others that are paid under the Department of National Defence, by the RCMP, or even our own plan as members of parliament. In all these cases, nominally we have funds but in actual fact in the legislation we do not call them funds; we call them accounts, because we all know no money is put into any fund-it is simply a bookkeeping matter. We have legislation which says that those who are now working as public servants or as National Defence, or RCMP personnel, or as members of parliament pay something into the treasury by means of a deduction from their salaries. They pay it now in the knowledge that those who are now retired draw pensions. We who are now working know that when our time comes, we will live not on what we save, not on actual food, clothing, shelter and services which we put aside, but because in that day there will be persons who will be working and

December 17, 1976
Income Tax
producing goods and services, a portion of which will be allotted to us.
I submit that that is the realistic fact about pensions. It is not an idea that is unique to me or that only I happen to have. Some very learned people in the pension field, especially in the academic world, have written a good many documents on this question. Some of them have been prompted to do so because they see pension plans getting into trouble. A great many of them in the United States have got into trouble, private plans and public plans, such as the plan for the city of New York, and so on.
I think a lot of agitation in this country today by certain groups against the nature of public service pensions is the result of the fact that private pension people are afraid they will not be able to match what is being done in the public service, and they are probably right. My contention is that all is not perfect in the pension field in what we have done now and there could be trouble ahead, but the whole thing could be greatly improved if we would move more and more into public pension plans and into plans that are honest and realistic in the sense that they are pay as you go plans.
In point of fact, I think that this is how the Canada Pension Plan works. In that case, again, there is a so-called fund or account, unlike the situation with respect to old age security, but still the money is not there. It is not in a sock, a bag or a bank somewhere-it is figures on the books. By means of figures on the books we lend money to the provinces which they get at a low rate of interest. But I suggest that this whole composite pension complex that we have built up is not the simple, direct, honest kind of pension arrangement that we could have. All these funds to which people contribute, and the credits they get, are really just a means whereby it will be decided what each person's pension will be when he retires; but if you have a million dollars a year to your credit as a pension, and if there is not a society at that time producing wealth on a current basis, your million dollars will be of no use to you.
As I say, I think that private pension plans in this country will not solve the problem in the future, nor do I think RRSPs will solve it. I think a great deal larger old age security pension and a great deal larger Canada Pension Plan will solve these problems, and my hope is that the retirement pension committee, or whatever it is that the minister refers to, the committee which represents three departments, is studying this whole question.
My question, therefore, to the minister is in two parts. On the one hand, is the committee studying the idea of a greater use of public pension plans and a greater use of the pay as you go principle; and, secondly, what are the minister's comments on the views I have been expressing?

Mr. Chairman, the committee for the study of retirement income is doing so in the broadest sense, so that its terms of reference are not limited; but, very obviously, the future expansion of public as opposed to private pension plans is central to its study.

I suppose the most difficult question hon. members have had to deal with in this pension debate has been the question of the indexing of public service pensions. I am inclined to say to the critics that it seems to me that their objections fail to come to terms with a rather more fundamental issue in our community; that rather than taking away the opportunity to keep the pension in real terms to wherever the economy takes it, we should be concerned about the fact that many private plans do not have this, so that private plans being sold now will not yield in real terms what the participant is expecting. This is a matter of real concern.
Conversely, another matter of concern is that a very substantial part of the investment capital which is made available for private investment in Canada is produced by an aggregation of different kinds of private plans, and in that sense to move it all into the public area would deprive the private sector of investment capital in the future.
They can always borrow from a public bank.
The hon. member says that the great, all-seeing government could lend them the money.
They could borrow it from a bank.
My preference would be to leave a maximum amount of enterprise in private hands.
That is a change.

On the question of accounts in terms of private funds, I take it the comments of the hon. member are really about public funds, but in terms of private funds the private firm does not have the expectation-I was going to say "assurance"-of continuity that a government has. It does not have the expectation that in 30 years, when a person retires, it will still be there and will be in a position to pay, as the government does. Therefore, it is to give security to the participants in the private sector that the funding requirement has been imposed.
I think it is artificial to talk about the public service superannuation fund as a fund. It really is an account, and I think there is a basic value to having a separate account because it can be better known how much of the federal government's over-all operations are devoted to retirement payments to its employees. I concede to the hon. gentleman that this is on a pay as you go basis. The specific term of it is that the participants, as they may be from time to time, are going to have to increase their contributions to have funds available, but I think it still is valuable. I have to confess that since the hon. member opened the discussion the other day I have not reread the exchanges between himself and the hon. member for Eglinton, but it seems to me that these are the principles which apply.

Mr. Chairman, first I should like to welcome the words used by the Minister of Finance when he defended the public service superannuation
December 17, 1976

plan, and in particular when he defended the escalation features which have been built into that plan. I hope I do not twist what he said when I say that I think what he was saying was that if there is a difference between public plans and private plans, the thing to do is not to take escalation away from the public plan but to build escalation into the private plans.
If it can be done.

The implication in that answer is that it is very difficult, and I am prepared to admit it is difficult. That is why my colleagues and I think we should move still further in the direction of public plans. The vehicles are there. The two main acts, so far as the general public is concerned, the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan, are right there waiting for a government with progressive ideas to move forward. I see the minister smiling at the suggestion of a government with progressive ideas. I suppose he realizes that that refers to somebody other than himself and his colleagues.
The minister said that to move more into public pensions is to deny the private sector the use it makes of the funds which are accumulated by private pension plans. Well, that is exactly what we think ought to be done. We think that if there are to be accumulated savings in terms of dollars or figures by the people of this country, the use of those accumulated savings should be for social purposes, and it should be decided by the people through their government rather than by private interests. So, in my view, on all counts we should be moving in this direction, but I stress again what I said a moment ago, without standing here and indulging in criticisms of the private sector, which we can do at the drop of a hat.
You have been criticizing it for years.
You can do that with the public sector, too.

We can do better in the public sector, too. I want the public sector to do better, and I want the public sector to provide most of the pension security. There are plenty of articles being written, not just by writers who think as I do, but by persons concerned about pension plans who are afraid that down the road the pensions will not be there or that they will not meet the needs. I can see private plans in trouble simply because they try to operate on the basis of funding and on the basis of irsing those pension contributions to make money, and so on. Whether they are contributions or deductions, they should be for the purpose of building up pensions and should not be simply a vehicle which financial manipulators can use to make money. Because of the problems down the way, I really think changes should be made.
I am glad there is this interdepartmental committee. I think we in this country have done much better in the pension area than has been done, for example, in the United States. I am not going to make the speech I make fairly often about who
Income Tax
pressed for these things to be done, but the fact is that the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan are good legislation. However, the fact that they are good just invites the government to move forward and to increase the amounts under the Old Age Security Act, to increase the amounts provided under the Canada Pension Plan and to let the dependence on private funds that cannot meet the bill wither away, if you will.
So it is my plea that this matter be given very thorough study. I am glad that the terms of reference of that interdepartmental committee are very wide, but I suggest that there is urgency to the matter, and when we are discussing RRSPs on clause 1, they are not the answer. Neither are private pension funds the answer. What is the answer is a greatly extended use of public plans and more of a realization that pensions really are on a pay as you go basis.
The minister said that a private firm cannot be sure that 30 years down road it will be able to pay the pensions in the way a government can be sure that 30 years down the road there will still be a government. I like to think that not only governments will still exist 30 years down the road but also society. This is a country and, after all, the production of wealth is a social process. It is done on a current basis, and if we face up to these facts we can have real improvements in what is now a pretty good pension scheme but which could be a lot better in terms of improvements both in the amount paid under the Old Age Security Act and in the proportion that the Canada Pension Plan is of the total retirement income of our people. However, I welcome the one or two good things the minister said. I hope the views which have been expressed today and the views expressed by the hon. member for Eglinton will be studied very carefully by the interdepartmental committee and that before very long its recommendations will be reported to us.

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to ask the minister a question as a result of some representations which have been made to me by individuals who purchased annuities with tax paid income. They are now collecting on those annuities and are being taxed again on the principal and interest which is, in effect, double-taxation. My understanding is that the trust companies they are dealing with informed them that the Department of Finance insists that this be done. Can the minister advise me on this matter?
Mr. Chairman, I am advised that in the case of a purchased annuity the capital portion of the payment is tax-free.
Is there any instruction to that effect? These people have had information from the trust companies involved that this is not so. I always understood it was so.
Mr. Chairman, section 60(a) of the Income Tax Act covers this.

Mr. Chairman, my question is supplementary to that asked by the hon. member for Edmonton West regarding

December 17, 1976
Income Tax
double-taxation in cases where in any year individual taxpayers have paid an excess into their RRSPs. 1 have letters from several people; as a matter of fact, I received one this morning referring to the matter. As I understand it, if you make an overpayment into the plan, the tax department adds the excess on to your taxable income for the year and you pay tax on that amount. If, and when, you withdraw it you are taxed a second time; in other words, double-taxation.
According to a letter I received this morning, the gentleman had an overpayment of $1,014.76 and his total tax was $880.70. He went to court about the matter and writes that it was admitted in court by the tax representative that this a problem of several hundred taxpayers and he comments that they are still required to pay it. In the past I have written to the minister's predecessor, but I have not had a satisfactory answer. It seems to me a very unfair situation where an individual is taxed doubly on the same amount of money.

Mr. Speaker, the basic principle is the one I cited in response to the hon. member for Edmonton West. In effect, inherent in the program is the provision that you should not be able to subtract from your taxable income an amount in excess of the maximum. I should say a more particular aspect of this program is dealt with under clause 56 of the bill which will change the situation in the past where if a contribution is made to an RRSP which exceeds the amount which can be deducted from the taxpayer's income, there is no way the overpayment could be returned to the taxpayer without destroying the plan. Clause 56 gives relief from that so that subject to limits it may be returned to the taxpayer.
Will this be retroactive?
It will be applicable to the 1976 tax year and thereafter.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to address myself to clause 1 which relates to the fact that the increase to $3,500 and $5,500 will create a windfall reserve of investment capital which will be in the hands of banks, trust companies, insurance companies and credit unions. I am not opposed to that; I think it is necessary in our economy. If the private sector is to operate properly, it must do so with the help given by the investment market.
I am concerned, however, that the same kind of consideration is not given to charitable organizations. There seems to be a general attack on the virtue of charitable donations. I recognize that the Income Tax Act increases the deductibility, and that is good; but there seems to be a growing campaign to make the government responsible for all the humanitarian services that are necessary in this country. Just last weekend a former premier of British Columbia said that the united good neighbour fund ought to be disbanded. I think that is ridiculous. If people no longer have the opportunity to donate on a humanitarian impulse, then we have become completely computerized and dehumanized.

I should like to ask the minister whether the opportunities could not be broadened so that other reputable and established organizations could take part in this windfall reserve of investment capital that will come to the private sector as a result of these funds. I am thinking of the established religious denominations, established missionary organizations and established private educational institutions. Is there any reason why such organizations could not participate in RRSP programs and become beneficiaries of this pool of capital? This would accomplish two things. On the one hand, many people would like to invest in a retirement program which has been very helpful to a lot of people.
To the wealthy.

I wish my socialist friend would listen to everything. I know he listens in a hyphenated way. There are people who would like to invest in a retirement plan but object to reinvestment. They do not like it when a bank takes their money and reinvests it in Labatt's breweries or some such institution. They would like to see their money invested directly in the capital programs of their church organization or missionary organization or educational institution. Why should they not have that opportunity and continue their charitable programs through their retirement program?
Second, when the institutions I have mentioned embark on a capital building program, they have to go to the lending institution and borrow the money at 1 per cent, 2 per cent or 3 per cent higher than they would pay if they could participate in the RRSP program. Why should they have to pay those extra percentage points to the large banking institutions?
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock p.m.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, just before one o'clock I was saying that when institutions like those of private education, churches or missionary societies want capital for expansion, they must borrow money from banks, trust companies or credit unions at interest rates 1 per cent or 2 per cent above the prime lending rate. Moneys which lending institutions lend are partly acquired from registered retirement savings plans.
My point is that, sad to say, since governments are impinging more and more on the operations of these institutions, it is becoming increasingly difficult for charitable and similar organizations to borrow the money they need. Since charitable and church institutions ought to be, and are, the means for maintaining a high moral and ethical tone in society, I say we should help, rather than hinder them. Obviously, if such institutions are to be given the right to participate in the
December 17, 1976

RRSP program, the provisions governing them must be the same as those governing other institutions and ought to include actuarial safeguards.
I know the Minister of Finance has worked for some time to establish new guidelines for charitable organizations and trusts. They are long overdue. Mr. Chairman, I think the parliamentary secretary would concede that there are two purposes to this plan. One is for the benefit of the person wanting a retirement income. That is what gives viability to the program. The second purpose is to provide a pool of capital which would be useful to the investment community. I am not criticizing that aspect. The private sector needs this capital if we are to enjoy a healthy and growing economy.
At the same time, we have to admit that as soon as a participant of a retirement program invests his money in a

I wish to return to a subject which several of my hon. friends have raised, that is, the whole question of how these various provisions for tax savings or tax postponement affect the total system of the collection of taxes which are required to meet the needs of the Canadian people. I have expressed my feelings about the operation of the RRSP and other pension plans. I wish to refer to what has been said by my hon. friend from Waterloo-Cambridge and my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands about the minister's apparent decision to drop the surtax on taxable incomes above a certain level.
The minister said, in reply to a question last year, that the surtax was part of a package which was put together because people with lower incomes were not getting the increases which they would have got as a result of the indexing of family allowances, so it was felt it would be fair to place this extra tax upon those with higher incomes. Since the escalation of family allowances is now to be resumed, it was felt it was fair to drop the surtax on people in the upper income brackets.
I do not suggest for a moment that the minister was not technically correct in his answer, but it seems obvious to me that the surtax was part of the whole package which the Prime Minister announced in October, 1975. The people were told that in order to deal with rampant inflation it was necessary to set up an Anti-Inflation Board and impose restraints covering price increases, wages and salaries, and not just wages and salaries but the incomes of other groups as well. As a matter of fact, the Prime Minister, on the first day he broached the whole idea in his speech on radio and television on October 17, 1975, stated:
No one will be permitted an annual increase of more than $2,400. I want to make it clear that the income guidelines apply to all forms of income including fees charged by doctors, lawyers, accountants, engineers and executives.
He could not have been more specific. Then the Minister of Finance, in December of 1975, I believe in the course of his meeting with the provincial finance ministers, had this to say on the same subject:
In terms of equity it is, we believe, only fair that those at the upper end of the income scale, who are able to absorb the impact of rising living costs without undue hardship, should be asked to shoulder some share of the burden ... It is fair to ask those who already enjoy ample means to make a proportionately greater sacrifice in the national interest.
Hon. members will know that the NDP members of the House opposed the anti-inflation program because we said it would not work, that it would not be fair and equitable. We were reproached very strenuously by the Minister of Finance and other members on the government side. We were asked why we did not go along with the NDP government in Manitoba which supported the anti-inflation program.

It is no secret that we disagreed with the government of Manitoba's position. The Premier of Manitoba was one of the first supporters, long before this government got the idea, of an incomes policy for Canada; but the Premier of Manitoba found that an incomes policy would work only if'it were applied fairly. He had the illusion that the government meant business. He had the illusion that the government would live up to the kind of commitments made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance which I have just quoted. Ever since then the government of Manitoba has been trying to get the federal government and the Anti-Inflation Board to live up to the commitments they made.
However, we know that the government has not lived up to its commitments. Doctors, lawyers and engineers are getting far more than an increase of $2,400. The Anti-Inflation Board, in its annual report, has given figures showing that this is so. The government of Manitoba tried to put a limit of $2,400 on the amount doctors would be able to receive in the form of a salary increase in any given year, but it got no support. In fact, its efforts were sabotaged completely by the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, who I am sure was working in close co-operation with the Minister of Finance.
It seems to us, Mr. Chairman, that removal of the surtax is one more illustration of the fact that this government never believed in implementing an incomes policy which would be fair and equitable. There is very little equity-in fact, it is inequity-in saying to people at the bottom of the income scale that their increase can be as high as $600 while people at the top of the income scale can get an increase of $2,400. We said at the beginning, Mr. Chairman, that the amount of the surtax was far too small. We said there should be a 100 per cent tax on income increases of more than $2,400.
What has this got to do with the bill?
It has everything to do with the bill.
We are talking about RRSPS.

We are talking about income tax, which is one of the largest sources of revenue required to meet the needs of the people of Canada. If you give concessions in the form of RRSPs and give away several tens of millions of dollars in the form of bonuses to people who avail themselves of RRSPs, then obviously you have to collect the same amount of money from some other tax source. It is for this reason that we object to the removal of the surtax.
Let me remind members of the House that it is because of the kind of policy the minister has adopted in removing the surtax that the Premier of Manitoba has announced that in all likelihood the Manitoba government will withdraw its support of the anti-inflation program, so far as public servants are concerned, in the coming year. Removal of the surtax will mean additional bonuses for the highest income group in Canada, a saving of $800 for those with a taxable income of $50,000 a year, a saving of $1,850 for those with a taxable income of $75,000 a year, and a saving of $3,000 for those with a taxable income of $100,000 a year. This is over and

The Toronto Globe and Mail and the Toronto Star over a year ago reported-I am speaking from memory, but I think I am correct-that there were at least five people in Canada over the last year, the "last year" being either 1973 or 1974, with incomes of over $200,000 and who did not pay one cent in income tax.

We believe that to rescind the surtax is another indication to the ordinary people of this country that the federal government lacks any real commitment to the spirit of the anti-inflation program which it announced more than a year ago. On top of that, while the government refuses to do anything substantial in terms of making the income tax system more equitable, it is continuing its policy of easing the corporate tax structure. There is no question that the corporate tax structure has become easier, while corporate profits, despite what the government claims, are substantially higher than they were a year or two ago.
Thank God.
The member says, "Thank God". That shows where his interests or his biases are.
The Canadian people are thankful for the corporate structure.

I would invite the hon. member who keeps interjecting to get up after I have finished and to put on the record his views on corporate taxes, at a time when the ordinary citizen finds it very difficult to pay the tax he is going to be asked to pay to meet the cost of services in this country.
For the benefit of the hon. member who has been interjecting, I will put on the record figures showing corporate profits. According to information compiled by Statistics Canada, in the first nine months of 1976, while in aggregate corporate profits have not increased-this, of course, is what we were assured would happen under the anti-inflation program- corporate profits in 1975 were approximately 2'/2 times their 1970 level, which was already exceptionally high. A more reasonable indicator of the profit picture is the rate of return on equity represented by current corporate profits. The federal government is using this concept to establish a minimum liable rate of return for corporations irrespective of cost increases. There may be considerable value in applying a similar test to determine whether profits are unreasonable or excessive.

An examination of the detailed information made available by Statistics Canada in the first half of 1976 to determine the return on the rate of equity garnered by the corporate sector in aggregate and in certain sectors shows there has been a very substantial increase in profit. Pre-tax profits represented a 20.4 per cent return in the mining industry in 1976, as compared with 11 per cent in 1970; 19.8 per cent in manufacturing in 1976, as compared with 10.7 per cent in 1970; 29.4 per cent in printing, publishing and allied industries in 1976, as compared with 18.7 per cent in 1970; 35.4 per cent in machinery in 1976, as compared with 11.6 per cent in 1970; 39.2 per cent in transportation equipment in 1976, as compared with 10.1 per cent in 1970; and 24.8 per cent in chemical industries in 1976, as compared with 12 per cent in 1970. I could go on, Mr. Chairman. In any event, the over-all total rate of return on equity for all industry was 18.3 per cent for the first half of 1976, as compared with 9.2 per cent for 1970.
These figures on corporate profits and on what corporate taxation contributes to the revenues of this country, together with the nearly $8 billion in deferred taxes which is really a no interest loan to the large corporations of this country, indicate that more than mere tinkering with the Income Tax Act is needed. On this note I am going to close. There should be a very substantial rewriting of the whole tax structure to provide for the kind of equity recommended by the Carter commission which was appointed by a Conservative government.
I again urge the Minister of Finance not to wait until the traditional time to introduce a budget, but to bring in a budget which will include income tax provisions that are fair to the ordinary people of this country and one which will give the economy the kind of spur it needs to get people back to work. This country certainly does not need 7.5 per cent unemployment. Quebec does not need 10.1 per cent unemployment, nor does Newfoundland need 13 per cent unemployment. The tax structure of this country, particularly the income tax structure, should give the economy a kind of boost it is not now getting as a result of the present Income Tax Act.
Mr. Chairman, my concerns are going to be addressed to the minister. They will not be in the form of instant economic solutions provided by the hon. member for Winnipeg North.
Be objective.

Mr. Chairman, I am advised that there is an option available here. The person in question could either elect to pay 25 per cent of his gross amount, or elect to be taxed as a Canadian, in which case he would have the full benefit of the personal exemptions that a Canadian taxpayer would have. This is with reference to the possible use of profit-sharing returns, in part in shares or in stocks, either purchased from a company or in a profit-sharing type of arrangement that workers might have with a company. Mr. Chairman, I have one final point to raise with the minister. I recognize the fact that this issue has been raised by a number of members, and I have also personally received a large amount of correspondence on the subject of annuities for people at the age of 70 or 71. I should like to refer the minister to page 2043 of Hansard where it is reported that the hon. member for Ottawa West directed a question to the minister which I think sums up pretty well the concerns of many members with reference to RRSPs. Could the minister perhaps elaborate on his answer? I recognize that he has not been able to commit himself definitely in that regard, but could he take a moment to review his answer and perhaps explain it in greater detail?

At the moment, the sole form in which the proceeds of an RRSP can be retained for pension purposes for retirement, other than getting a full pay-off, is by the purchase of a life annuity. The representations that we and members of the House have received from the participants in the plan have included the suggestion made by my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa West, that one should be entitled to keep those funds either with the same trustee or some other trustee, or be entitled to a payment of the income on those funds from the trustee during his retirement years, perhaps with some encroachment on capital, rather than by annuity. I can only reply by saying that there is now no provision in the law for that kind of arrangement. I am prepared to undertake to make certain that this matter is considered by the retirement income committee when it is under way.

Mr. Chairman, I have one final question for the minister with reference to the provision for roll-overs. I understand that the only option is an annuity. I do not suggest for a minute that I am an expert in this field, and that is why I inquire. Why cannot a person pay taxes on his RRSP if he cashes it in, either the entire sum or in part, if he reinvests it so that it brings in a higher rate of return? I must say that I do not agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he expresses concern regarding the savings instincts of Canadians. I think it would be unwise to direct our concerns to a spending economy rather than a savings economy in the long haul. I think that all Canadians to some degree would have the proper motive. Is there anything wrong with their paying their fair share of the tax, whatever the government sees fit, but not going the route of an annuity? Let them choose their own avenue of investment, somewhat as described by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock.

That is an option that a participant in the RRSP now has. In effect, he can take the entire proceeds of the plan at the age of 70, but of course he would have to pay tax on the full amount. He would be able to average his tax under the income averaging provisions of the

bill, but there would be tax payable. At that point he is free to invest as he likes.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on Bill C-22, to amend the Income Tax Act. There are a number of provisions in this bill about which 1 have a great deal of concern and to which I take some objection because in my opinion some of the amendments proposed only perpetuate some of the inequities in our personal income tax system which discriminate against low and middle income Canadians, to the advantage of upper income Canadians. For this reason I would like to outline, first of all in a general way, my philosophical reasons for objecting to some of these clauses, and then to get into some specifics and deal with some of the amendments before us.
In any income tax system that any government imposes, there seems to be an obligation on the part of the government to have some kind of fairness and equity in the system so that groups and different sectors will bear the burden of taxes in proportion to their ability to pay. We have in this country the personal income tax system and the corporate income tax system. What has been happening to various tax policies of the government-and the bill before us today is only the latest example-is a change in the tax burden, in who is shouldering this burden.
What has happened, for example, is that over the past couple of decades we have seen a change in the way that the corporate sector bears the tax burden and the way in which the person or individual citizen in Canada has to pay taxes. For example, in the 1951-1952 fiscal year we find that about 54 per cent of the income tax collected by the federal government came from the corporate sector, and about 46 per cent of taxes came from personal income taxes. But a couple of decades later, by 1973-74, this proportion had changed dramatically, for in that year, the latest for which statistics are available, we find that about 30 per cent of income taxes came from the corporations and about 70 per cent came from individuals.
So a great shift has taken place in the income tax system. The burden has been shifted to individuals, to the personal income tax system and away from the corporate income tax system. The point is that this shift has come away from the corporate sector to the personal income sector at the same time that corporate profitability has been increasing, and hence their ability to share the burden has been enhanced. We find, for example, in the last five-year period from 1970 to 1975 that corporations' profits have increased from $7.7 billion to $17.8 billion, or an increase of 131 per cent. But during the same period of increased corporate profitability the corporate tax rate declined from the effective rate of 29.6 per cent to 26.6 per cent.
Estimates show that because of the tax concessions, the write-offs and the loopholes, the federal treasury has been losing some $2 billion to $3 billion a year in terms of the corporate tax revenue that it could be collecting. On top of this kind of inequity there has also been another provision which has allowed corporations to postpone or defer paying income taxes, a provision which is not available to individual Canadi-
Income Tax
ans. To date we have the astounding figure-they are estimates, but based on the rate of deferral-that corporations have been able to defer or avoid paying the federal treasury some $10 billion in corporate income tax. That is a very significant sum. We do not even charge interest at the going rate on this deferral of some $10 billion. It is, in effect, a free loan; but you know very well that if I were to be late in paying my personal income tax, I would be charged interest on it.
The argument for this reduction in the corporate tax rate as well as the shift of the tax burden away from corporations to personal income taxes has always been that this will stimulate the economy and create more jobs. What a hollow and false argument that has proved to be. We find that some 700,000 Canadians are unemployed today. Obviously, the tax concession method is not working to promote a healthy economy for Canadians. The point is that we have a system of taxation which has built-in inequities with regard to the corporate and personal income tax systems which are further compounded when we analyse the trends which have been taking place within the personal income tax system itself. What I am trying to show is that the burden has been shifted away from corporation taxes to personal income taxes, and within the personal income tax system the burden is being shifted away from those in upper income brackets to those in lower and middle income brackets. RRSPs are only one example of the inequities that are taking place in our income tax system.
Do poor people buy RRSPs?

A number of studies have been carried out recently. One of the most recent and most significant was done by the National Council of Welfare, a government advisory body set up by an act of parliament. The study shows that because of a number of newer exemptions and deductions, some of which are in this bill today, and because of modifications being made to these deductions, taxpayers earning under $5,000 per year get an average tax saving of about $244, but taxpayers earning over $50,000 per year save about $4,000 because of registered retirement savings plans, income interest deduction plans and all the other deductions which are built into the system.
The point I am trying to make is that we are moving away from the idea of a fair income tax system based on one's ability to pay. What is fair about a tax system which permits 27 per cent of all tax savings to go to the top 5 per cent of income tax filers and only 33 per cent of tax savings to tax filers with low and middle incomes who, of course, make up the majority of taxpayers in this country? That is not a fair system, and this was pointed out in the report of the National Council of Welfare when it tried to define what would be a fair tax system and what principles should apply. The provisions of the bill before us should adopt those principles. I think it would be useful to examine the amendments before us within the context of the definition found at page 4 of the report, which is as follows:

Any discussion of taxation must begin with two fundamental concepts: the progressivity of the tax structure-what percentage of income is paid in taxes- and the comprehensiveness of the tax base-what is included as income in computing taxes.
This, basically, boils down to the idea that the more you earn and the more you can afford to pay in taxes, the greater is your ability to pay. Page 5 of the report-and I agree with this wholeheartedly-states:
The rationale behind the ability-to-pay principle is that government has a right-in fact, an obligation-to modify, through the tax system, the great disparities of wealth which arise from the unequal distribution of income. In other words, the tax system ought to be, and in fact is, an essential part of our system of income redistribution. It collects money from those who can pay and, through this collection, makes possible those other programs which provide a basic income to those whose own income is insufficient for their needs.
I think all Canadians agree with this principle, and it is one of the ways in which we have been operating-or supposedly operating-our tax system date. For example, this is the concept behind old age pensions. When people retire and are without the amount of income they have been used to, through our tax collection system we are able to supplement their incomes because we have been taxing people according to their ability to pay. Surely this is what the system should be all about, and surely this is what the amendments we have before us should be doing. But when we look at them in detail, we find that that is not the case. We find that although many Canadians think our income tax is regressive, the tax rates vary from province to province in terms of personal income tax rates, and in terms of the federal system, from a low of 7 per cent to a high of 63 per cent.
The point is that those figures can be very misleading and many Canadians think that this is the rate at which they are being taxed, but it is not that way because when we take into account deductions and other loopholes, we find that the progressivity, which is so important to a fair taxation system, is not there. One of the good examples of this is the interest income deduction plan. We find, in that the plan allows the first $1,000 of interest not to be taxable, the benefits of this deduction go to higher income Canadians at a much greater rate than to people on lower incomes. For example, quoting again from the report of the National Council of Welfare on page 28:
The savings of the average taxpayer were to be encouraged, it was said; but once again the greatest benefits went to the wealthy. The figures show the same pattern as with all the other tax subsidies; persons making between $5,000 and $10,000 received an average tax saving of $39.06; those making between $10,000 and $15,000 received an average of $56.39. Those earning $25,000 to $50,000, however, received an average benefit of $216.01, while taxpayers who made over $50,000 got, on average, $339.40.
In other words, we have a plan here which is supposed to save people's money, but the unfairness of it is that it benefits the wealthy who already have more income, and hence more protection against inflation and rising costs. It benefits them to a much greater extent than it benefits low and middle income Canadians. In terms of lost revenue in 1974, the last year for which statistics are available, this interest income deduction plan cost the treasury some $550 million. Surely there is a far better way to redistribute income than using that $550 million through the interest income deduction plan to give greater
[Mr. Symes.J
benefits to the wealthy. Surely we could have used that money to devise a better scheme and give greater benefits to lower and middle income people who are fighting so hard to survive the growing inflation rate.
We see this kind of example in government legislation. Tax benefits help the wealthy more than they help lower income Canadians. For example, with the registered retirement savings plan we find the same pattern emerging. The figures produced by the National Council of Welfare are very revealing. It is argued that this plan is necessary because it will give people an incentive to put money away for their retirement. No one can quarrel with that concept. Surely, however, because the people on the lower and middle income scales will face more severe problems when they retire in terms of income than upper income Canadians, the system should be revised in favour of them. This plan works exactly the opposite way; it gives benefits to the wealthy. The amendment will give larger benefits to upper income Canadians because it raises the amount they can contribute.
Let us examine some of the figures, Mr. Chairman, as given at page 23 of the report of the National Council of Welfare. For those earning under $5,000 a year the tax saving from this registered retirement savings plan is $1.02, but only 38 per cent of tax filers belong in that group. Those earning between $5,000 and $10,000 save $9.81; they represent just over 31 per cent of tax filers. The average tax saving for people earning between $10,000 and $15,000 a year is $38.43, and they represent 18 per cent of tax filers. In the group earning between $15,000 and $20,000 a year the tax saving jumps to $125.01, yet they represent only 6 per cent of tax filers. When we come to the group earning over $20,000 a year, the tax saving takes a tremendous jump to $551.88, yet this group represents only 4 per cent of tax filers. Where is the fairness in this system? Is it taxing people on ability to pay? It is not.
The personal income tax system has been so warped by the policies of this Liberal government that the more a person earns the more he can save through programs like this. I have not heard any Conservative oppose this backward step.
