provisions that have been added over the years to the Income Tax Act, such as the deferred cash payment on prairie grain delivery, that have been of assistance to farmers in averaging their income, another plan that has been of great assistance is the five-year averaging provision that has been in place for some time. I would suggest to the minister, however, that improvements are still needed to bring in better equity in income averaging for farmers. The tax laws for the most part are designed primarily for the wage earner with a fairly steady monthly cheque and fairly steady annual income which hopefully increases as the years go by. Farmers, on the other hand, have never been able to look to a uniform annual increase so I would hope that the minister would consider extending the five-year averaging period.
I do not believe that the cattle industry is treated as fairly as the grain industry under present legislation. We have all seen situations where cattle are bought in December or January purely for the purpose of beating the tax situation. I do not think a law should be set up that encourages buying cattle, or deferring buying them as it has in the past. I think there is room for a provision that would enable a cattle producer to sell off a significant number of his herd and put the money into a special averaging annuity which could be drawn as income over the next several years. I am aware that there are provisions in that respect for anyone who discontinues a farming operation, but surely there is no reason why such a scheme should not be available to anyone who wishes to continue farming but decides to get out of the cattle business, for example. Changes have been suggested by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association which has had requests along these lines from cattlemen, particularly in western Canada, during the past year. I wonder if the minister could tell the House whether his department is considering such changes to Bill C-22 and, if not, would he consider it for the future?

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for his representation. Similar suggestions have been received from time to time, but the judgment has been made that the five year period is adequate. I am prepared to re-examine the question, however, to see if it might be appropriate under the circumstances he has described.

I hope the minister will examine that, Mr. Chairman. In my view the present provisions are not adequate to make a fair income averaging generally available to food producers, particularly the cattle industry.
I should like to deal with one further aspect of the tax act not specifically before us today. I have raised the question of the capital gains tax with respect to farm consolidation. I have had a number of situations drawn to my attention during the last year or so in which a farmer who owned six quarter sections of land, say, had the opportunity to buy two quarters close to his home base of operation. In the situation I have in mind he did not want more land; he considered selling two quarters which were perhaps 20 miles from his home and buying two quarters close to home. In other words, he would
Income Tax
wind up with the same amount of land and a more closely knit farm operation. In the meantime, because he would have sold the distant land, he would have incurred capital gains tax. I realize that it may be difficult for the minister and his officials to suggest a provision which could apply fairly in that situation. However, it is a situation into which we run with increasing frequency in western Canada owing to the rise in the value of farm land since valuation day. Has the minister given this matter consideration and, if so, can he make any comment to encourage my constituents who have encountered such problems?

Mr. Chairman, there are no people in Canada whom I would like to encourage more than the hon. member's constituents. I ought to point out to him that in past considerations this has been a most difficult area. Talking in the most general terms, the statute now provides for roll over possibilities where there has been an involuntary disposition of land, for example, where there has been an expropriation and where property passes on death, under certain circumstances. Representations have been made not only with regard to farm land, but with regard to equities in businesses and other major assets; those have been representations for exemptions and up to now it has been difficult to concede on any one of those examples without conceding the principle of the legislation as a whole. I have undertaken on a number of occasions to take a fresh look at the matter, but at the moment I would hesitate to ignite any spark of encouragement for thinking that there will be immediate action at this point.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief. I apologize to the Chair for not having been present during the entire debate in committee, and the point I am about to raise may have been dealt with. I wish to make a suggestion concerning registered retirement savings plans. It seems to me that, basically, those earning reasonable incomes invest in such plans in order to escape a certain amount of taxation in the years they invest in such plans. But many complain because present programs are restrictive and do not yield as good a return as they might. Is it possible for such funds to be put aside, by the simple expedient of depositing them, for example, with a trust company? When the funds are withdrawn the owner would be issued, say, with a form not dissimilar to the T4 for regular income or the T5 for security income. It could be a form of that kind. The point is, you could use such a form in any year subsequent to the year of original investment, so that once the money is taken out, tax would be paid on it.
A man may want to retire early. Perhaps he has a terminal disease and knows he will not live long enough to benefit from the retirement funds he has put aside. Or perhaps the depositor has no terminal disease; perhaps he or she does not feel well and, at some age before retirement, decides to call it a day and pack it in. The saver who has money put aside is not eligible for old age security but may be prepared to use some of his laid aside funds and pay tax on them. His income in the years before he gets the old age security pension will be

December 17, 1976
Income Tax
relatively low. It seems to me that people like that should be able to withdraw their funds and pay taxes on them. Presumably such people would not withdraw this money when their income is high and would withdraw it only when their income is at a low point. When the money is withdrawn the trust company, bank or other institution would issue the T slip as I have suggested in the year in which the withdrawal is made, and that money would be taxable. In other words, the owner of the money would pay tax in that year, or on that part of the money he withdraws.
All or any part of it?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: On all or part of it, yes. It seems to me that such provision would allow the depositor to negotiate interest terms with the financial institution receiving the deposit. He would have complete control of his funds and, if an emergency arises in his life, he could control his financial destiny by using all or part of these funds, and pay the taxes applicable. I have put forward a suggestion. I wonder if the minister would comment on it, or say why such a simple plan could not be worked out.

Mr. Chairman, I canvassed this point on page 1626 of Hansard. It has been a recurrent theme throughout this particular discussion. In essence we are talking about a retirement plan rather than a savings plan. It is a retirement plan which would make the position of the registered retirement savings plan person analogous with that of the registered pension plan contributor.
The solution the hon. member proposed deserves to be dubbed the Ottawa West solution, after my colleague from Ottawa West who suggested that-
Is he still your colleague?

-instead of having to invest the money in an annuity, it should be possible to invest these funds and continue them in a trust relationship with a trust company, withdraw the income, and perhaps anticipate on some of the capital, rather than bring the program to an end. I would have to say that that is one of the matters with which the study into retirement income will be concerned. In the past we have really only tried to analogise the registered pension plan with the registered retirement savings plan. But the question naturally arises as to whether we might consider some different arrangement. I might conclude that remark by saying that the individual participating in a registered retirement savings plan has the option of taking all his money out and paying tax on it in that one year, under the income averaging provisions.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: But not a portion of it?
Not on a portion of it at this point.

Mr. Chairman, I have a flight to catch at four o'clock and wish to say a few words. I understand from my colleagues that we may continue this debate on Monday,

so that perhaps I can conclude my remarks in two or three more speeches next week.
We will be happy to extend the time.
But not the aircraft.

There lies the difficulty, Mr. Chairman. I do not have available the aircraft privileges extended to the Minister of Transport.
I am interested in what the hon. member for Kootenay West said. He described the difficulties of a man in his community who had worked 20 years for Cominco and retired on a pension of $125 a month. He finds the 25 per cent tax he must pay the Canadian government difficult to bear. It seems to me that the problem is not so much that he must pay 25 per cent as that he collects only $125 a month after working for that mining company for 20 years. It seems to me that is a fairly good argument for indexing pensions, and it is an indictment of that company's private pension plan, since it will not support this man when he most needs support, in his retirement years. Hon. members who recite such stories always look at them from the private sector point of view, which does not work at all.
What does work?

What works? The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre outlined an excellent program for pensions in this country. If the minister and the official opposition would listen to him, the people of this country would be well-served by such a plan.
A reading of clause 1 makes it evident that at a time when the regressive nature of the tax system has never been so well-documented, a further retrograde step is being taken. It is incredible that the government should choose to introduce a bill which goes further toward entrenching inequality in the national tax system. It is ironical that a government which claims to be in favour of the principle of progressivity should introduce a clause such as this. These are times when I wish there was television in the Chamber so as to show that when an important bill such as this one is under consideration, most of the Tories have gone off for the weekend-
Where is your party?
-or else they are hiding on the back benches and writing their Christmas cards, while poor people have to exist on a pittance.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Merry Christmas, Rodriguez!
What are you doing with your $1,500 raise?
Order. I think we should listen to the hon. member for Nickel Belt.

I can understand the sensitivity shown by some members. If I were doing these things myself, I would be upset. At least they woke up in a hurry.
The principal of progressivity implies that the proportion of income which an individual pays in taxes should increase as a person's income increases. When the government accepted the ability-to-pay principal, it theoretically committed itself to doing something about the great disparities of wealth which arise from the unequal distribution of income. Supposedly it was going to collect taxes from those who can pay and then use that money to provide programs which increase the income of those who cannot make ends meet.
If the Liberal government were even the least bit committed to a principal which the majority of Canadians believed in, one would have expected to see the gap between the poor and the wealthy narrowed. But given the government's record of doing exactly what it promised it would not do, it is not surprising to learn that income disparities have actually increased in the last few years. According to Statistics Canada, the lowest quintile of the Canadian population actually received a lower share of total income during 1975 compared with a year earlier. When the 3.9 percent recorded for this sector of the Canadian population is compared to the 4.4 percent obtained by this group in 1965, it becomes possible to see how "progressive" the Trudeau administration really is. As the Globe and Mail stated on October 21, 1976:
The figures suggest that despite government efforts to redistribute income with family allowances and other transfers to individuals, low-income groups are still receiving a lower share of total income than during the mid 1960's before many social welfare policies were improved.
The poorest 20 per cent of the Canadian population is not only becoming poorer, but is also bearing the greatest tax burden. The tax system as a whole does nothing to contribute to the goal of income redistribution. As Allan Maslove states in a report for the Economic Council of Canada,
Indeed, over the lower portion of the income scale, the system tends to contradict the ability-to-pay principle by taxing the poor at a higher rate than those who are better off.
In this report entitled "The Pattern of Taxation in Canada," Maslove shows that the over-all effective tax pattern is highly regressive to a broad income level of $5,000-56,000.
I hope the minister will comment on all this, because I want to know how it is that despite all the tinkering with the tax system in the past few years we have not narrowed the gap between the rich and the poor in this country. I want the minister to explain this to me, because the people in my riding who live in inadequate housing and receive inadequate incomes want to know the answer. I hope he will be able to explain, so that I can send out copies of Hansard and let them see the answer.
I hear another interruption from over there. The hon. member should be concerned about it, too, because the part of the country he comes from, northern New Brunswick, is not exactly the lap of luxury.
Given that 46 per cent of all family incomes are included in the under $6,000 income class, according to 1969 statistics, the
Income Tax
regressive tax structure affects a very large proportion of the population. He also points out that 8.3 per cent of family units which received $15,000 income in 1969 paid at a rate of 8.4 per cent less than those earning under $2,000. Furthermore, the highest income group paid a lower proportion than did the average. The extreme regressive nature of the tax system at the low end of the income scale and the lack of progressivity over the remainder is the overriding conclusion to emerge from Maslove's study.
On top of all this, it is clear that the wealthy are not paying higher taxation rates through the corporate sector. In fact the corporate contribution to the total tax revenue has been rapidly declining in recent years. As R. Deaton writes in "The Fiscal Crisis of the state":
Between 1962 and 1970, the corporate share of all federal income revenue fell by roughly 38 per cent while the additional share of federal income tax revenue increased by over 23 per cent. With respect to all provincial income tax revenue between 1962 and 1970, the corporate share fell by over 60 per cent while the individual share increased by roughly 83 per cent.
In full knowledge of these facts, what is the government proposing to do? It hands us a piece of legislation which does not contain a single clause which will make the tax system even slightly progressive. In actual fact it is attempting to implement measures which are of benefit only to middle and high income earners. The government is purposely deviating from the principal of progressivity by providing tax deferrals and loopholes.
While the present system of tax brackets and the corresponding marginal tax rates have the appearance of being progressive, in actual fact the progressivity of the tax system is a myth. All those provisions in the Income Tax Act for reducing taxable income are only of real benefit to the affluent. The government is actually subsidizing the rich instead of using that money to provide programs for the poor. As "The Hidden Welfare System" points out, "these tax subsidies provide the greatest benefits to the well-to-do but are of no benefit to those outside the tax system because their incomes are too low." This amounts to institutionalized inequity, or as we on this side of the House call it, socialism for the rich.
Clause 1 of Bill C-22 is one more step in the direction of entrenching inequity in the Canadian tax system. This clause illustrates the problem about which I have been talking. Clause 1 limits for RRSP contributors have been raised from $4,000 to $5,500 for those who do not have a pension plan, and from $2,500 to $3,500 for those who do have a plan. This cannot be supported for several reasons. First, the poor, those with incomes below the tax payment threshold, receive no benefit from the program in terms of a tax saving. They cannot save $1,000 let alone $3,500 to participate in this program. These band-aid retirement programs provide no old age security for the poor.
Secondly, the wealthier the person, the greater the benefit. As the National Council of Welfare found in 1974, persons earning over $20,000 received four times the benefit of persons

December 17, 1976
Income Tax
earning between $15,000 and $20,000 and 14 times the average benefit of persons earning between $10,000 and $15,000.
Finally, in 1974 the RRSP program cost Canadians $513 million. This money could have been used to develop programs for those in need of assistance rather than to provide tax shelters for the rich who are the friends of the government and the Tories in this House. They do not need any extra retirement benefits. Do not tell me that L. Edward Grubb, former president of INCO, on top of his $150,000 a year pension needs an RRSP. He needs it like I need a hole in the head.
This sort of proposal by the government is a prime example of the kind of fat cats it looks after. It looks after its own friends, Mr. Chairman. It does not look after the poor of New Brunswick or northern Ontario.
What about Toronto?

It does not look after the poor of Toronto either. That, in a nutshell, Mr. Chairman, is the philosophy of this government: the rich get richer under this program and the poor get poorer. You cannot argue with the facts.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Nickel Belt accept a question?
Certainly. I recognize that any answers I may give may help the poor in New Brunswick so I will let my hon. friend ask his question.

It would help the people of New Brunswick, whether they are fortunate or not, to have the hon. member admit this. Is he aware that it was the Liberal government in the 1960's that introduced to this country a national program of medicare; and does he believe that it was the fortunate in society who benefited most from that program?

I am glad the hon. member raises that question. It is obvious he does not remember his history, and a man who does not remember his history is lost. It is obvious who introduced and endorsed medicare in this country.
Who introduced it?
This is another example, Mr. Chairman, of a party that has principles, a party that has a social program. We dragged this Liberal party kicking and screaming into the twentieth century.
Who was it that kept the Liberal party in power? Why did you support them in 1963?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I think it would be only fair, as I said a while ago, to hear the hon. member for Nickel Belt.

In further answer to the hon. member's question, he knows full well that it was a CCF government that put medicare into Saskatchewan. When Thatcher of the

Liberals took power in Saskatchewan he started dismantling the program and placed a fee on users of the service. The Liberals were kicked out and have never returned since, and good riddance to them.
Those are my remarks regarding this part of the discussion on clause 1, but I will return, Mr. Chairman. My colleagues have assured me that I can return next week, and we will still be here later next week.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one can have a lot of fun with statistics and I do not think anyone has more fun with them than the hon. member who has just spoken. But the one positive statement that he made which is totally false and which, among many others, I would challenge him on was his assertion that in this country over the recent period the rich have gotten richer and the poor have gotten poorer.
I do not want to address myself to the gap issue, the question whether the gap between the rich and the poor is broader or narrower, because that is less important. What is important is the fact-he is not in a position to deny it because it is true-that the poor in this country have been getting progressively better off. Perhaps the gap is not closing fast enough, but that is another question.
One of the things that I and other members of this party are proudest of is that the poor in this country have been progressively getting better off. In 1968, according to the Economic Council of Canada, 18 per cent of the people of this country were living in a condition that the Council described as poverty. In 1976 that figure had been brought down to 11 per cent. That is still too many people in Canada living in poverty; but for him to tell the House that the poor have gotten poorer is totally false. I hope he is man enough to stand up in his place and acknowledge that what he said is not true, that in fact there has been steady progress made in Canada, though perhaps not as much progress as he or some of us would like. Nevertheless, it is false to say that the poor in this country have been getting poorer.
Mr. Chairman, I listened carefully-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I recognize the hon. member for Nickel Belt but I would appreciate it if hon. members would confine their remarks to the bill before the committee.

Then I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I think that since I was accused of making false statements and I was challenged on them, I should respond to that. I am glad the hon. member mentioned this, and I am glad that what he said is on the record. I want him to tell me whether there are five million Canadians living in poverty. Are not things relative? The cost of living is an indication that these people have not moved ahead in terms of the buying power of their dollar. I would like him to stand up and tell me why the five million poor of this country have not had their conditions improved; why on Indian reserves we have 90 per cent unemployment. Let him not tell me that the Indians do not count,
December 17, 1976

because they sure do. They are Canadian citizens, Mister. Indians living on Manitoulin Island-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I think the hon. member for Nickel Belt recognizes that he is not raising a point of order but merely a point of debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will take but a couple of minutes of the time available to us to raise an issue that is somewhat associated with the comments made by my colleague and good friend from North Battleford. It comes under the provisions of the Income Tax Act as it affects the capital gains tax on farm land.
There has been representation made over the years to the effect that there is an inequity between farms that are not incorporated being allowed to be transferred within the farm family for farm purposes and, in so doing, escape capital gains tax. That provision is not extended to farms that are incorporated. Perhaps in the past there was good reason because, generally speaking, incorporated farms have another business associated with them. It might be an egg grading station, trucking company, cattle sales barn operation, and so on.
I do not want to ask a question but just put forward the suggestion that in the review of income tax, as given by the minister to the hon. member for North Battleford, he will also consider the possibility of exempting from capital gains tax that portion of the incorporated farm that is land only. This would seem to make it fair for the non-incorporated farm and meet one of the objectives that we all have, that this country be as self-sufficient in food as possible.
If that is not done, one of the risks we run is on the larger farms, the ones that tend to be incorporated, the management team and often the basic herd are broken up for tax reasons. Not only do we lose the land from productivity, but also the management, and the people engaged in agriculture go into some other vocation.
I simply wanted to take that minute to raise my concern that we also look at rolling over only the land portion of incorporated farms as we do for non-incorporated farms, but certainly not any associated business. In that way we protect against the request by all small businesses that they have the same provision.

Mr. Chairman, it is always interesting to sit in this House when the hon. member for Nickel Belt is speaking. It is also interesting to note the kind of reaction he seems to inspire. If he were making an argument that was not worth listening to, and if his facts were inaccurate, I would expect the kind of dull silence we usually have in this place on a Friday afternoon.
It was interesting this afternoon to watch the reaction from both government members and the official opposition. Why do they get so upset at the poor old hon. member from Nickel Belt? He is just a poor little guy from the back woods who comes here to say a few things, but everyone gets upset. I
Income Tax
suspect that he touches a nerve when he comes into this place. There may be a conscience starting to rise.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I thought the hon. member for New Westminster was rising to discuss the bill before us. If that is the case, he may continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. member will permit a question.
Of course, on any subject you like.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the argument of the hon. member for New Westminster is so cogent, Mr. Chairman, I would be delighted to know why his colleague from Nickel Belt did not stay in the House to listen to it.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Nickel Belt had a very important engagement with the poor people of his riding in Nickel Belt.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You are laughing, Stu.

He does not have "Air-Otto" to get him there. He has to travel by regular aircraft. That means leaving here at least half an hour before his plane goes. He has every right to leave this place on a Friday afternoon. I am delighted he was able to stay here long enough to get members opposite so excited. It is nice to see some of the oldtimers in the House actually open their eyes for a change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Stanley has his eyes open.
He said oldtimers.

The hon. member for Nickel Belt was well briefed. I expect he will be back on Monday to complete his remarks.
In accordance with your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I will get back to Bill C-22, Clause 1. It deals with the iniquitous problem of rewarding high income earners with more tax shelters than there are RRSPs.
There is a myth abroad that things like RRSPs have not affected the redistribution of wealth. We have quoted a number of statistics which amply demonstrate that this is a regressive measure. What is happening with RRSPs is that you are distributing income in reverse. That is why we have taken a firm stand in terms of eliminating these kinds of tax shelters and why we favour the Carter commission approach to taxation.
Along with that kind of myth is the idea that somehow, because of the so-called progressive tax system we have, corporate wealth is being redistributed through the corporate tax structure. I want to deal with that for a minute because it is related to Clause 1.

David Lewis did it.

Income Tax

A lot of people did it. They are no less accurate and they are no less correct.
It took the Royal Bank of Canada 100 years, from 1870 to 1970, to accumulate $11.4 billion in assets. In five years under this government, represented by the Minister of Finance, the Royal Bank went from $11.4 billion to $25.2 billion. That is an increase of $13.8 billion, far more than they accumulated in the entire previous century. The idea that somehow this government, or a government formed by the official opposition, is too hard on business is absolute nonsense. There has never been a more friendly government to large business in Canada.
There is nothing wrong with that.

I can understand someone saying there is nothing wrong with that, because we stand in this House with a different philosophy. That is why there is a failure to perceive the basic thrust of the argument we are making about income tax. It is exactly the argument that my good friend, the parliamentary secretary, made. He said we should not forget that the poor are not getting poorer, the poor are probably getting slightly richer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I did not say probably, I said they are.

I accept that. I think it is correct, but it does not deal with the disparity, and that is what you must deal with in a society that is falling apart at the seams. Crime rates are rising. These are relative facts. The relativity is that one person may be going to Hawaii or the Barbados where he will have a great time, while the other person is struggling away at home. He sees that the sweet life is available to everybody but him. That fellow is a great candidate for being a bankrupt. That is why I suggest members opposite fail to perceive that the thrust of income redistribution is where the basic difference lies between the parties of this House. It is income fairness, a redistribution in terms of society, that holds a society together. I will take you to any modern, western industrial society where income disparity is not as high, and I will show you a lower crime rate.
A country like Sweden.
You betcha!
And like Great Britain.

Yes, like Great Britain. I do not mind Great Britain at all. It is a nice place to live in, and I don't know why the hon. member for York-Simcoe is against Great Britain; it is a lovely place. These Milton Friedman economists cannot get it into their heads that there is something in civilization besides the almighty buck.
Let me get back to what I think is the interesting answer given by the parliamentary secretary that he did not care so long as the poor got relatively less poor, or at least that their incomes came up. He misses the entire point about the subject that is now under discussion in this committee. There is no
fairness in this tax system under which we live. I will give you another example, that of the little fellow who runs a gas station, the small businessman.
The amount of tax that the government collects from small business operators of gas stations is far higher than the tax collected from the corporate giants that lease those stations. Is that fairness? This guy is being driven to the wall with self-service stations, he is being driven out of business, and he also has to pay more than his fair share of the tax. That is why, unless you perceive the argument which is to redistribute income and to have a genuinely progressive tax system, there is no point in us shouting back and forth at each other because we are on two tracks, one going right by the other.
Hon. members are making an assumption in their arguments with the hon. member for Nickel Belt that they can abandon the whole concept of income redistribution. If they would all just admit that they are against income redistribution and that they wish the rich to get richer and to see disparities in income grow, we would not need to debate the subject any further. That is the only answer we can perceive from the answers they give.
What is wrong with both the poor and the rich getting richer?

There is nothing wrong with it, but we should reduce disparities in incomes.
I should like to go back to the bill and I want to ask the minister or his parliamentary secretary to respond to another question which is typical of what I see as an elitist approach to the tax system. A wage earner who has his tax deducted at the source does not have any advantage, through interest or otherwise, because of the moneys that are deducted in advance in anticipation of what his tax burden will be in any particular year. A professional or a corporation can file his or its income tax on a quarterly basis. Why is there that distinction? I am asking this question seriously and I hope the minister or his parliamentary secretary will put his mind to it.
Why is it that, for example, the government allows use of those funds for at least a quarter in the case of the corporation or professionals, whereas a wage earner has to have it deducted on a monthly basis? Why is there discrimination between wage earners and professionals? It is clearly to the advantage of corporations and professionals to do it that way, and clearly to the disadvantage of those who work with their hands to do it the other way. If I am wrong, I will be happy to be corrected. It is typical of the whole philosophy behind the government's approach to income tax. As a lawyer I can pay quarterly. In fact I can pay at the end of the year, if I want, and then there is a slight penalty involved.
The official opposition look at it in exactly the same way as does the government. It is largely as a result of the poor not having the kind of political clout and political power that resources give one in the kind of society we have. I hope I can have an explanation of that kind of discrimination, but I must say that it is somewhat typical of the approach to taxation
(Mr. Leggatt.]
December 17, 1976

which this government takes. The RRSP, as we were arguing, is clearly a discriminatory provision.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Can you keep this up for another three minutes?

I doubt it.
I want to deal with something else in clause 1, which is the discriminatory feature of RRSPs in terms of the tax shelter given the rich. What has been needed for a long time is the direction that Carter, a very conservative accountant, recommended a long time ago, that is, to tax money as it flows, to tax money as it is available. I have never been one who believes in universality, and I will disagree with many members of my party on that question. I think that is wrong.
Why?

Because R. J. MacMillan should not get a guaranteed old age pension. He is in a position to provide his own. Income tax does not take it all up, and that is the argument that we have been making. The income tax system is not progressive enough to take it all back.

speechtext:
In the first debate back in 1973-and I trust hon. members have had an opportunity to consult Hansard- the intention was to set out goals for rehabilitation. I summarized at that time what these goals were in the words of a member of the British House of Commons, Alfred Morris, who has since become the Minister for Rehabilitation in the present British government. I quote Mr. Morris again as follows:
We seek a society where there is genuine respect for the handicapped; where understanding is unostentatious and sincere; where if years cannot be added to the lives of the very sick, at least life can be added to their years; where needs come before means; where the mobility of disabled people is restricted only by the bounds of technical progress and discovery; where the handicapped have a fundamental right to participate in industry and in society according to their abilities; where socially preventable distress is unknown; and where no man or woman has cause to feel ill at ease because of disability.
That is much more than the bed and pension approach which prevailed far too long in dealing with handicapped Canadians.
One of the great leaders in the rehabilitation field in Canada was the late Keith Armstrong who, as founder of the Canadian

Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled, provided, I think, the greatest leadership of all who have been engaged in this field. Dr. Armstrong passed away last June 25, just as we were moving into new dimensions in the rehabilitation movement, but he has left a great heritage. During his career Dr. Armstrong stressed co-ordination, and pointed out time after time that while Canada was rich in facilities for dealing with rehabilitation, while there was a multiplicity of voluntary agencies-no less than 48 voluntary agencies, as far as we can discover-and while there were all sorts of highly skilled individuals working in this field, there was a great need for co-ordination and co-operation if we were really going to get the rehabilitation movement going as we desire, and as this motion today suggests we should.
I am sure Your Honour will agree with me that there are exceptional skills in the rehabilitation field. My interest in rehabilitation is much more than the interest of a member of parliament; it is because of a personal involvement originally and because of personal problems in the family. More recently it is because I myself have been the beneficiary of the skills of rehabilitation medicine. It was just a year ago that Your Honour and myself were under the care of one of the world's most skilled surgeons in the field of cardiac rehabilitation, Dr. Wilbur Keon.lt is significant, Mr. Speaker, that this is the same gentleman who was the key person involved in the more tragic circumstances surrounding the former Leader of the Social Credit Party, whom we remembered in this House today.
By 1975 it was remarkable how much progress had been made. After just two years there had been much improvement and development, and I reported this in a statement I made at that time. One of the major areas of activity was the technical aids committee set up by the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled. I had become increasingly involved and I had the privilege of being appointed chairman of that committee. Its essential work was to make available as quickly as possible sophisticated electronic equipment for the severely disabled and chronically ill. This would also spill over to the geriatric population.
In 1974 a seminar was held in Vancouver by the Kinsmen Rehabilitation Foundation. This was a major breakthrough on the North American continent because it provided a format for making the equipment available, an action that is urgently needed to get the handicapped population out of expensive human warehouses and institutions and back into the bosom of the family and into the community. The report of the seminar, an excellent publication, was made available to the government. This is still the only basic document we have that provides information on activity in this field.
Other workshops have been taking place. As recently as last August professionals working in the field were brought together at the Crippled Children's Treatment Centre here in Ottawa for an educational and informational seminar. Similar seminars will be held in Edmonton and the maritimes next
December 17, 1976

year. As a result of the leadership provided by the Canadian voluntary groups in this field, an international seminar will be held in Seattle next June.
Out of all this priorities have emerged. It is now recognized that there is an urgent need for an educational information centre in Canada where all the professionals working in the field of rehabilitation can find information on how to best carry out their responsibilities. Dr. David Symington of Queen's University is chairman of that subcommittee on educational information; Miss Margret Perry of the Kinsmen Rehabilitation Foundation is chairman of the subcommittee on distribution of the systems. She is not only Canada's leading authority but has an international reputation as well. The subcommittee on engineering and development is chaired by Nelson Durie of the National Research Council; that committee is compiling information on equipment available, as well as carrying out development and engineering. The subcommittee on evaluation and standards is the responsibility of Professor Robert Scott of the University of New Brunswick.
Canada needs a national information centre not only for public education but also as a resource centre for professionals. It will eventually be necessary to have a similar centre in each of the provinces as well. The education of professionals in regard to rehabilitation skills is being pioneered at Queen's University under the direction of Dr. David Symington. He has an excellent program there which will become the prototype for similar educational and training programs in universities across the country, in addition to community colleges and other centres of education.
The big problem is funding and working on the basis of ad hoc funding. There is a great need for advisory councils. The province of Ontario is providing leadership in this and has an advisory council made up mostly of handicapped persons. Perhaps, too, one day we will have a minister of state for rehabilitation as they have in the United Kingdom.
Many developments are contemplated for the future. Recently a seminar was held in Toronto on the employability of the handicapped, which was sponsored by the federal and provincial governments and private groups. It was found that rather than being a liability to places of employment, handicapped persons were an asset. Speaker after speaker from industry pointed out that because of attitude and aptitude and to the job devotion the handicapped person was often a more profitable employee. It is expected that the result of the seminar will be a great leap forward in employment of the handicapped. The Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) spoke a few minutes ago, Mr. Speaker. He is not here at the moment, but he will be interested to know that the Post Office is opening up employment to handicapped persons who are adept on the coding machines which are necessary in the automated postal service.
A seminar was held in Edmonton last see week on housing, transportation and support services for the handicapped. The report of that seminar will be available to the general public, and of course will be directed to government at all levels. It should be pointed out that most of the funding for these
Handicapped Citizens
seminars and workshops is made available by the federal and provincial governments.
Another development that is encouraging is the cross-fertilization of many agencies in the field of rehabilitation. Many members of this House attended the legislative breakfast held on October 13 by the Canadian Association for the Mentally Retarded where the president, Margot Scott, did an excellent job of presenting the needs of the association. CRCD is also getting into an area of concern and international responsibility through co-operation with ICTA, the International Commission on Technical Aids, Housing and Transportation. We are working and co-ordinating with the Prosthetic and Orthotics Association and the Biomedical Engineering Society to avoid duplication.
A CRCD delegation, which included the former parliamentary secretary to the minister of national health and welfare, was in Tel Aviv last June to make an appeal to hold the next international congress on rehabilitation in Canada in 1980. We were successful, and Winnipeg will be the host city in June, 1980. At that great gathering experts from all over the world will meet for a whole week in an effort to solve the problems of the handicapped. It will also be the end of the decade of rehabilitation. That, of course, will be the basis for international attention and celebration, and Canada will be the focus.
In the background of all this activity has been the Department of National Health and Welfare. The message has come through loud and clear from the minister, because on May 13, in response to some of the representations from the groups I have mentioned, particularly the handicapped themselves, he said:
In every area the message was clear:-
He was referring to the handicapped people. I continue quoting:
-They 'wanted in': into employment, into community living, into maximum participation in community life, into the planning of systems and services designed to help them. At the same time they 'wanted out': out of institutions, out of dead-end sheltered workshops, out of welfare, out of being pitied, out of being thrust onto the sidelines with a pension and a shrug.
That shows that the minister is in tune with what is going on in the country. I trust-and I am coming to the end of my remarks as I wish to allow time for other contributions this afternoon-that we will be able to agree that one of the best ways of bringing this all together, of bringing this about, is through a committee which could deal in depth and broad dimension with all the activities taking place, a committee whose work would place Canada in the forefront of the rehabilitation movement in time for the activities of 1980. It would also be a good Christmas present for the handicapped. I suggest, too modestly, that after 25 years' service in the House of Commons this year, it would be one of the best rewards a member of parliament could be given.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION COMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate from the bottom of my heart the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) for bringing forward this motion, and for his courtesy and generosity in allowing me to second it. His genuine concern for the handicapped transcends partisan politics, which are usually petty. He has shown genuine concern for our fellow human beings, fellow-Canadians, particularly those who are weaker than others. I commend him on his concern.
I do not want the motion to be talked out and will do my share by keeping my comments brief. I should like to point out some facts which perhaps the hon. member did not have time to point out. May I refer to the Declaration on the Rights of Disabled Persons which was co-sponsored in the United States by Canada? Incidentally, this declaration of rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on December 9, 1975, little more than a year ago. I should like to quote two paragraphs, because they illustrate that about which I am concerned. Paragraph 7 reads:
Disabled persons have the right to economic and social security and to a decent level of living. They have the right, according to their capabilities, to secure and retain employment or to engage in a useful, productive and remunerative occupation and to join trade unions.
That paragraph highlights an omission or gap in service which became noticeable in the seminar to which the hon. member referred, a seminar on the employability of the handicapped help in Toronto. There the message was clear. The handicapped said, "We do not want handouts; we want work and we are capable of working." The question is, how are we to get them to their place of employment? What means of transportation are we to use? It is easy to say that, yes, we shall give them a job. How are they to get to that job? Remember, these people to a large extent pay the same taxes which you and I pay, particularly for public transport. But what is public transport, expecially in Toronto, doing to help the handicapped? The answer is, unfortunately, very little.
Some other Canadian cities are giving the handicapped better service than Toronto is giving. For instance, recently

when I was in Halifax I noticed a special bus which is especially equipped for the handicapped. It was provided by the generosity of one human being, not by that of any government. I suggest that we should look into this kind of thing. The gap in services is enormous.
My second point concerns paragraph 12 of the Declaration, which reads:
Organizations of disabled persons may be usefully consulted in all matters regarding the rights of disabled persons.
I would not have drafted that paragraph in that way, for to say the least it is patronizing. I would have rephrased it and said, "Organizations of disabled persons should be usefully consulted in all matters." That is the crux of the matter and explains my slight hesitation with respect to this motion, excellent though it is.
The point is, we must find out the real needs of the handicapped. They do not want our pity; they do not deserve it. But they do deserve our help. We must know how best to help them, and who will decide that. Will it be a group of bureaucrats who know nothing of the handicapped and feel that, while looking down on them, they are under the moral obligation of feeling affection for them as they would for Tiny Tim? No, we have gone beyond that, surely. The handicapped themselves must tell us what they need. We must have the guts to follow their recommendations, and not impose on them our ideas. That is one of my reservations.
Although reference to a committee has been recommended, I think it would be an excellent idea to establish a subcommittee, since in all probability its members would at least know about the problems of the handicapped. They would be receptive to ideas concerning the handicapped. I hope that such subcommittee, or special committee, would invite as many of the disabled as possible to come before it to testify; in that way we could learn from the handicapped. We cannot presume to know the answers. We should be humble enough to ask them what to do.
I return to the question of the employability of the handicapped. Not long ago I placed a question on the Order Paper asking how many people officially designated as handicapped were employed by the federal government. If one excludes the Department of National Revenue, the numbers were not impressive. I am not proud of them. I am certainly not proud of the record of all federal departments. We must consider this question carefully. Are we not wasting time and merely paying lip service to ends we want to accomplish?
One year ago, when speaking on a similar motion proposed by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, I strongly recommended that a ramp should be built so that Canadians in wheelchairs would have the opportunity to listen to debates in the House of Commons. Although they have the same privileges as other Canadians, they do not have facilities for coming into the galleries of this House. I raised the point one year ago. Where is the ramp?
I raise another point. Are federal buildings, particularly Canada Manpower Centres, readily accessible to the hand-
December 17, 1976

icapped? Not on your life! 1 raised another question one week ago and was told, with a little patronizing pat on the back, that a five-year study is under way to ascertain how many Canada Manpower Centres are accessible to the handicapped. A five-year study! In the meantime, what happens to people who are in wheelchairs and who really want a job? How are they to get to the officials of Canada Manpower? Are they to telephone? With due respect to Ma Bell, it takes a lot more than a telephone conversation to get a job nowadays. There is an appearance of good will, but in real terms what we find is a shrug and total apathy.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION COMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak on the motion of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) with respect to the appointment of a joint committee of the House and Senate, or of a sub-committee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, to study the needs of the handicapped and the services available to them.
Before I begin my comments I should like to express the regard and admiration I feel for the hon. member for Brandon-Souris who, over the years, has worked so indefatigably for an important group in our society, the handicapped. Last year when the hon. member presented a similar motion, the occasion was marked by the presence in the Speaker's Gallery of most of the members of the committee on technical aids for the handicapped, some of whom had to be carried up the stairs to the gallery because they were in wheelchairs. The reason they were available to attend was that they had just come from a meeting of their committee, a standing committee of the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled of which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris is the chairman. I understand he was in Tel-Aviv this past summer, along with the former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the hon. member for York-Centre (Mr. Kaplan). During that visit he helped to ensure that in 1980 the World Congress of Rehabilitation International will be held in Canada; to be exact, in Winnipeg, a city which I understand is quite close to Brandon, part of the constituency represented by the hon. member who has presented this motion today.
The three efforts I have just mentioned are only the three most recent ones; there have been many others over the years. In this instance, because of the hon. member's contribution to the cause of the handicapped, I feel I can break with tradition and pay compliments to someone on the other side of the Chamber. And since I am throwing bouquets this evening I should like to express the view that the hon. member's motion is intrinsically a valid one, just as last year's motion was intrinsically valid. Had I seen this motion three or four years ago, I think it is quite likely I would have gladly supported it.
Last year the hon. member's motion proposed that a number of services be made available to handicapped persons. At that time the government was able to state that a great many of the needs identified in the motion would be met through the provisions of a shared-cost agreement with the provinces, an
Handicapped Citizens
agreement which would help the handicapped in two important ways. First, it would offer cost-sharing to the provinces with respect to more comprehensive rehabilitation services affecting a broader group of persons, including children and the aged. Second, it would offer the provinces cost-sharing, or improved cost-sharing arrangements which would permit the handicapped, the aged also, to remain in their own communities rather than move into institutions. I believe we have convinced the hon. member, because this year he has not repeated this particular part of his motion. I feel sure, from the feedback I am getting, that many groups in Canada today have recognized the proposed legislation as a step in this direction. More recently, at the annual meeting and conference of the Canadian Association for the Mentally Retarded, support for the legislation was evident.
I would at this point beg the indulgence of the House while I quote from remarks made by the president of the association in response to an address by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde):
The proposed federal Social Services Act has much to commend it to the Canadian public. Most noteworthy is the intent of the legislation to preserve the dignity of all persons in need of social services and to assure the provision of such services in a way which would preserve traditional family and community living patterns. This approach of delivering services is most encouraging to the Canadian Association for the Mentally Retarded.
I think all members will agree that the government has come a long way in three years toward meeting the needs of handicapped citizens. I am speaking specifically now about the proposed cost-sharing legislation in the area of social services which I understand will be receiving first reading in the House in the new year. I, for one, look forward to taking part in the debate concerning this legislation.
As most members are aware, the legislation is a positive result of the social security review which has been going on with the provinces for some three years. All Canadians, including the handicapped, were invited to join in the review, and many of them did. Moreover, the government actively sought the views of a number of organizations which speak for the handicapped. A survey of the needs of the handicapped was carried out and I understand, from the information contained in that survey, that the needs identified were closely related to what was contained in the motion which was before us last year.
All this is to say that we already have sufficient evidence as to what the needs of the physically and mentally handicapped are. That is not the problem we face today. Indeed, I understand that the handicapped are beginning to feel over-studied and over-surveyed. One investigator, I am told, was recently thrown out of a club because the handicapped members were tired of answering questions. They wanted action. Mr. Speaker, the kind of action they want will be possible once the legislation of which I have been speaking reaches the implementation stage.
I should like now to be more specific with regard to some of the benefits of the proposed legislation, benefits which are not available either under the Canada Assistance Plan or the vocational rehabilitation for disabled persons programs.

Handicapped Citizens
A better range of rehabilitation services will become available for handicapped persons whose ultimate goal is employment. This would include employment-related services such as employment preparation. It would also include services to help disabled persons keep the jobs they have found-counselling, structural modifications to the place of employment, and, perhaps most important, transportation services to and from work at a reasonable price. A related area would be the establishment of a fund to permit capital expenditures for rehabilitation facilities. It is hoped the fund would encourage the setting up of innovative kinds of facilities, training grounds for the employable handicapped which would resemble small businesses and be vigorous and stimulating places for the rehabilitation process.
The legislation would not lose sight of the disabled persons who cannot work-obvious examples are disabled children and the elderly with handicaps. Included also would be a number of persons whose multiple handicaps make the regular labour market an impossible goal. I make this last statement guardedly because every day we hear of miracles-of mentally retarded, blind people, for example, being trained for jobs, and of new technical aids making possible today what was impossible yesterday.
It is equally important for such persons to be able to enjoy the benefits of living in Canada, to have the kinds of services that the "employable" disabled enjoy. The vocational rehabilitation of disabled persons legislation featured employment as the sole criterion for eligibility. This would be dropped in the proposed legislation in favour of making it possible for all handicapped persons to become eligible for rehabilitation services. For children this would mean special day care services, prostheses and medication; for the elderly it would mean a range of necessary counselling and social integration services; and for the elderly and others there would be the same transportation services to community activities as are available to the employed to get to and from work.
In addition to rehabilitation services, a number of what are termed "support services" would be shareable in order to enable the handicapped and the aged to remain in their own homes. At the present time the only alternative for a large number of them is to go into some kind of institution, a home for the aged, a chronic care hospital and so forth. Is it logical for some people to have to obey a nine p.m. curfew just because they live in a hospital instead of an apartment? People should be able to choose where to live. If they choose to live in a community and contribute to it, then they should be able to do so, and the community should be able to provide the kinds of services that are necessary to accomplish this end, whether that be day care, homemakers' services, attendant care and other services. Again, the legislation which will be before the House would make it possible for the federal government to share in the costs of such services when the provinces provide them.

I do believe, though, that the second part of the motion now before us has more validity than the first part, namely, preventing duplication of services by providing better information. I also believe that there is need for a great deal more information on the topic of rehabilitation and disability in Canada and that it should be possible to have access to this information more easily than is now the case. Certainly there should be more published information available on what is happening in Canada before we host the 1980 World Congress.
I believe that the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled some time ago asked the Centre for Applied Research and Engineering Design at McMaster University to do a study with respect to the feasibility of establishing a national information centre for the handicapped. The centre reported that there was a definite need in Canada for this kind of service.
I am sure you will understand, Mr. Speaker, that this is a complex matter. The handicapped and the professionals working with them have need of a wide range of information. A doctor at a rehabilitation hospital, for example, might want to know about new developments in the area of artificial limbs. The occupational therapist might want to know where to find a lightweight feeding spoon for a person with cerebral palsy. The handicapped person might want to know where he can find an apartment he can get into with a wheelchair. How would you provide for such diverse requests?
In addition, some information is needed on a national basis-information, for example, on artificial limbs, wheelchairs and other aids. A lot of other information is required on a local basis: where to get homemakers' services, what theatres are accessible, meals on wheels, and so forth. Other information is required on a more regional basis: where is the closest school for the deaf, what association can help someone with multiple sclerosis? Not all of this information should be stored in a national centre. Housing for the handicapped in Thunder Bay is of interest only to persons in and around Thunder Bay or-and here is the catch-a handicapped person who intends to move to Thunder Bay. If it is impossible to store local information in a national centre, it will still be necessary to be able to have access to that kind of information somehow.
To complicate matters further, it would seem that one of the most pressing needs, at least as far as the handicapped themselves are concerned, is to know more about services. And services will be the most difficult subject to grapple with. They are basically a local responsibility delivered by local voluntary agencies or municipalities and funded, in whole or in part, by the provincial government which, in turn, is reimbursed 50 per cent by the federal government.
There may be a partial solution in that, within the proposed social services legislation, cost sharing would be available for information and referral services at no cost to the user. Certainly information and referral services for the handicapped would be included. It is to be hoped that the federal legislation would permit wider usage of such services in Canada on local and provincial bases.
December 17, 1976

In addition, I am gratified to learn that the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled is prepared to take up the challenge and to pursue the matter of information for the handicapped. Apparently a committee has been formed and a proposal is forthcoming, I believe.
It would seem that the hon. member's motion is not really necessary in that in the proposed social services legislation we have one of the most important opportunities of helping Canada's handicapped which is apt to pass our way for some time. I suggest that we use it. I also suggest that all hon. members and Senators who are interested in helping Canada's handicapped should reserve their energies for debating the bill which will come before the House right after the new year, at which time, of course, witnesses can be heard and the whole matter considered.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for bringing forth this motion which is most timely and of interest to many Canadians, particularly the handicapped.

His record as leader in this field, as a man of knowledge and personal experience, has uniquely qualified him to direct the attention of all of us to this most important matter. I strongly support this impressive motion. I have been impressed by the remarks of ladies and gentlemen opposite. I was particularly impressed by what the hon. lady said about public buildings under federal jurisdiction, where for too long we have been too casual, careless, and thoughtless.
My colleague has drawn the attention of the House to a positive matter. It has often been said that government and the institutions of the nation should help most those who most need help. The motion before us is a very constructive one. I heartily support it and I am confident that this House, in thoughtful assembly here on a Friday afternoon, will support it as it goes to a vote.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION COMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the very outset I should like to extend my thanks and congratulations to the hon. member who has sponsored this motion, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who, I would say, perhaps more than any of our colleagues in this House, has been distinguished by a career marked by compassion and good work.
I feel the government has accomplished a great deal to date in this field of services for the disabled. However, as our country is evolving, the services should also expand to serve a larger target group. Society would benefit more if it could give to all of is members a better quality of life that would lead them to become more independent and participate in industry and in society according to their abilities.
The destiny of our handicapped has not been enviable, nor is it now. We must not fool ourselves: those considered physically handicapped represent approximately 10 per cent of the population. This group is highly diverse in terms of age, family situation, income, and types of disabilities. For centuries the
Handicapped Citizens
disabled have been objects of pity, but the handicapped have now come out of their isolation. They have stepped out into public view with their artificial limbs and in their wheelchairs. They are now pressing governments to be given their rights and to make their own contributions to the growth of Canada.
Too often, after being prepared at great cost to fill a role in society, the physically and psychologically rehabilitated handicapped person is prevented from doing so. So-called architectural barriers often frustrate the best laid plans. A couple of steps, too narrow an exit, a small room, and he or she becomes a prisoner, a dependent.
It must be recognized that the disabled, as well as us, the so-called able-bodied, need friendship, satisfactory jobs and incomes, recreation, transportation, housing and accessibility. Their efforts often fail because of the physical obstacles they must face in today's environment. For example, the ambulatory disabled find it difficult to use door knobs, stairs, and other common design features that make it possible for all of us to move around and live a normal life.
Many seriously disabled confined to a wheelchair cannot use public transportation, have difficulty in finding suitable accommodation, and satisfactory employment. These individuals must condition themselves to work for a low income and a way of life that has not much to offer as far as activities are concerned.
A large number of us are here this afternoon because of a mini-bus system which transported us from, say, the Confederation Building. Most of us can get to where we want to go when we want to go. We require a wide choice of modes of transportation and we want to be able to choose among them, sometimes the fastest mode, sometimes the least expensive and, at other times, the most scenic.
The disabled person does not have a real choice most of the time. In most areas, for example, public transportation is not accessible, although I understand one young man in a wheelchair in Vancouver got tired of paying the high prices of the mini-bus system and started using public transportation until authorities broke him of this singular habit. I am told that he wheeled up to a bus stop and waited for the bus driver or fellow passengers to help him on. Once on the bus, he held onto one of the posts toward the front of the bus and put on the brakes of his chair.
The only mode of transportation available to the disabled in the community is the taxi. The disabled have told me that not all companies and not all drivers are interested in driving the disabled or are physically able to handle a wheelchair. Some speak of waiting up to four hours for a taxi. For most disabled persons, and I would venture, for most Canadians, this is a mode of transportation which is prohibitively expensive. Yet there are many disabled persons who are forced to take taxis to and from work every day, thus increasing their work costs often tenfold. Many handicapped are locked into unemployment because they are actually unable to afford the cost of being employed. This is not a contradiction in itself. Who

Handicapped Citizens
could afford to work at a minimum wage job ten miles from home if the only transportation is a taxi?
A very small percentage of severely or totally disabled Canadians in the labour force receive their main source of income from personal employment. There are many contributing factors to this high unemployment rate, of which transportation is but one. Nevertheless it is an important factor, especially for those who are looking for employment. The availability and expense of transportation can be an insurmountable deterrent to employment.
An extensive American study on transportation for the handicapped, based on a survey of handicapped people, estimates that 13 per cent of the chronically handicapped aged 17 to 65 would return to work if transportation were no longer a problem. Transportation in itself does not create employment but it does create the conditions in which employment is attainable.
The handicapped require transportation services for reasons other than employment. Their trip purposes are just as diverse as for the non-handicapped, including trips for educational, medical, entertainment, shopping and recreational purposes, or simply to visit the home of a friend. Improved services would be invaluable in this regard as they would make possible the participation of the handicapped in all facets of community life. Increasing contact with the general public would facilitate the gradual elimination of long-held prejudices based on a lack of understanding of the needs, and more important, of the capabilities of the handicapped. This process is often referred to as normalization, the aim of which is to bring the handicapped back into the community on an equal basis with everyone else. It is a process which, if successful, will be of benefit to all, and adequate transportation is the first step toward its realization.
The implementation of the new social services legislation would enable the federal government to share in the costs to the provinces of providing transportation services to handicapped people, not only transportation to employment, but to visit doctors and to take part in community activities as well. I am sure that this new service will be greatly appreciated by the disabled and that it will help them to acquire more independence; they will no longer have to depend on friends or family to join their community. Whichever way we come to our purpose in helping the handicapped, I certainly hope we do.
I again thank the hon. member for Brandon-Souris for bringing this motion before the House.
